exhibits.title: The Two Maps
exhibits.text: A brass sphere with a flat pane of glass touching its north pole — and the instrument breathes. OUT: a straight arrow grows on the flat window, and as it lengthens its tip is laid down onto the curved brass as a great-circle arc — a GEODESIC, the straightest road the surface allows — travelling exactly the arrow's length, in exactly the arrow's direction. A flat straight step becomes a curved move that never leaves the surface: the EXPONENTIAL MAP. Then the reverse: the arc gathers itself back up onto the glass, leaving only the straight arrow pointing at where the journey ended — the LOGARITHM MAP. Arrow to arc, arc to arrow: the whole secret of arithmetic on a curved world is in that breathing.

exhibits.title: The Exponential Map
exhibits.text: Stand at a point p and lay the flat tangent plane there. Pick a tangent vector v — a direction and a length. exp_p(v) answers one question: 'if I set off from p along v and walk the SURFACE a distance equal to v's length, where do I land?' The road is a geodesic — the curved world's honest imitation of a straight line. Direction of departure: kept. Length: kept, now measured along the surface. Straightness: traded away. And the landing point is guaranteed to lie ON the surface, never beside it — that guarantee is why the map is treasured. Above: the gold bead takes the straight step; the blue bead walks the same length along the curve.

exhibits.title: The Logarithm Map
exhibits.text: The logarithm runs the exponential backwards: give it a surface point q near p and it returns the straight tangent vector that reaches it — log_p(q) = v, the v for which exp_p(v) = q. Its direction says which way q lies; its length is the geodesic distance. Together the two maps are a BRIDGE, and the crossing is a pattern you will use again and again: (1) LOG nearby points onto the flat window, turning them into ordinary vectors. (2) RECKON there — add, average, step — where vectors obey. (3) EXP back along a geodesic to a point that is once again perfectly valid. One honest caveat: the bridge is trustworthy near p and grows unreliable far away; for the small local moves arithmetic needs, exp and log are faithful inverses.

exhibits.title: Out to the Flat, Back to the Curved
exhibits.spec:
graph LR
  V[straight tangent vector v] -->|exp: walk the geodesic| Q[surface point q]
  Q -->|log: unwrap to tangent| V2[straight tangent vector v]
  V2 -.identity round trip.-> V
exhibits.caption: exp wraps a flat straight vector into a geodesic move onto the surface; log unwraps a surface point back into the straight vector that reaches it. Faithful inverses for small moves.

exhibits.title: Wrap and Unwrap, Measured Out
exhibits.caption: The simplest curved world — the unit circle of planar turns — with its flat tangent window at p. (a) The exponential as a promise about length: a straight step of length θ on the tangent becomes a geodesic arc of exactly length θ along the circle (here θ = 1.0 radian, landing at angle 1.0). (b) The loop closed: exp carries v = 1.0 to q = (cos 1, sin 1) ≈ (0.540, 0.841); log reads it back to 1.0, unchanged. Out to the flat, reckon in straight lines, back along a geodesic — always landing exactly on the surface.

exhibits.title: Where This Leads ↑
exhibits.text: Imagine every valid state is a point on a curved surface, and any move must land ON the surface, never beside it. You cannot add a straight vector to a curved point — the sum falls off the world. But you have the bridge: LOG the current point to the flat window, take the ordinary straight step there (a gradient step downhill, or a small nudge of uncertainty), and EXP back along a geodesic to a state that is perfectly valid. That is how gradient descent and tracking-through-time are done when the space of answers is curved — the daily craft of a hall not yet raised above this cellar. Master the two maps as pure geometry; the machinery will feel familiar the day the stair is built.
